Need to search first.I hit the tool limit before I could open most pages in full. Almost all of these notes come from the excerpts the search tool returned, so some sources are only partly covered. The notes on vv. 21–27 are thin.

## 2 Chronicles 30: research notes

**v. 1**
- Matthew Henry: Hezekiah invited the northern tribes for a religious reason, to bring them back to God, not to win them back to David's house. He says this was repaying evil with good, because the north had often troubled Judah. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- A commentator quoted on Bible Hub (not named in the excerpt) takes "all Israel" to mean northerners living in Hezekiah's kingdom. "Ephraim and Manasseh" stands for what was left of the ten tribes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/30-1.htm
- Clarke: it's hard to see how Israel's king allowed this, but Hoshea is generally counted one of Israel's better kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/2-chronicles-30.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): the letters could not have gone round the north without Hoshea's consent or at least his permission. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: the king decided this in council with his nobles and the people's representatives, probably before 14 Nisan. The law (Numbers 9:6–11) allows a second-month Passover in cases like this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Matthew Henry: Hezekiah feared that if he waited a year, people's zeal would cool. So he applied to the whole nation the Numbers 9:11 rule that was meant for individuals who were unclean. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- Dillard (quoted on Precept Austin): Numbers 9 allowed the delay for those defiled by a corpse or away on a journey. The Chronicler explains the delay by the shortage of priests and the lack of an assembly. The NASB Study Bible (also quoted there) mentions that Jeroboam had moved the north's festival calendar back a month (1 Kings 12:32). https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary
- Bible Hub Q&A: this applied existing law rather than inventing something new. It sees the "second chance" as a picture of Christ reaching those "far off" (Ephesians 2:13). https://biblehub.com/q/Why_celebrate_Passover_in_2nd_month_2.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: "at that time" means the first month, when the temple had just reopened. The cleansing wasn't finished until 16 Nisan (29:17). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Bible Hub Q&A: the second month gave time to consecrate priests and prepare. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_celebrate_Passover_in_2nd_month_2.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: the plan that pleased them had two parts: keeping Passover in the second month and inviting the north. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Dillard: the verse again stresses that king and people agreed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary

**v. 5**
- Ellicott reads the last clause as "not in multitude had they kept it": people had not been coming in large numbers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Barnes gives the same alternative reading, applied to the northern Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-chronicles-30.html
- The NET note gives the Hebrew literally as "not for abundance had they done as written." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/passage.php?passage=2Ch+30%3A1-6
- Precept Austin: "Beersheba to Dan" is an idiom for the whole land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary

**v. 6**
- Ellicott and JFB: the "posts" were runners, probably from the king's bodyguard. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- NET note: "so He may return" expresses purpose or result after the command to return. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/passage.php?passage=2Ch+30%3A1-6
- **Debated: had Samaria already fallen?**
  - The Expositor's Bible says the northern kingdom had already ended and only a remnant was left. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-chronicles-30.html
  - Barnes says the passage doesn't imply that. The "kings of Assyria" could be Pul, Tiglath-pileser and Shalmaneser. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-chronicles-30.html
  - Matthew Henry puts the siege of Samaria two or three years later. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
  - The Pulpit homiletics notes that Keil and others date the Passover to Hezekiah's sixth year, after Samaria fell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_chronicles/30.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: "your fathers" means Israel from Jeroboam on. "Your brothers" means Naphtali and the tribes east of the Jordan, whom Tiglath-pileser deported. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Matthew Henry: let their harms be your warnings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- The Restoration Commentary sees a distinction here between the leaders who sinned and ordinary people who couldn't stop them. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/2-chronicles-30.html
- The NET note quoted on Precept Austin: the word for "unfaithful" (*maʿal*) means crossing the line between common and holy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary

**v. 8**
- Ellicott links "stiffen your necks" to 2 Kings 17:14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Matthew Henry: "submit" is literally "give the hand," like sealing a bargain. Coming into covenant with God comes before communion with Him. Stubbornness is "bred in the bone" and has to be overcome. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/2-chronicles-30.html
- Precept Austin: Israel must draw near on God's terms, at the temple as the one place He appointed. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary

**v. 9**
- Matthew Henry: if you return to God in duty, He will return to you in mercy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- Precept Austin: *shub* is one of the verbs for repentance. The letter's "if… then" statements show that God really responds to our choices. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary
- Constable: if the north had fully repented, God might have freed many exiles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-30.html
- A Bible Hub excerpt: God's rich mercy is the great argument for repentance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/30-1.htm

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: the couriers went no further north than Zebulun, which he thinks makes the account look historically genuine. The verbs describe ongoing mockery. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- The Expositor's Bible: either "Zebulun" stands for all the Galilean tribes, or "Beersheba to Dan" is rhetorical. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-chronicles-30.html
- Matthew Henry: their scorn sped up their ruin and left them without excuse. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- Barnes: Ephraim and Manasseh were nearest to Judah, Zebulun one of the furthest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-chronicles-30.html

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: "humbled themselves" means repented. Verse 18 adds people from Ephraim and Issachar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Matthew Henry: God always has a remnant. Pride keeps people from yielding to God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- Morris (quoted on Precept Austin): a remnant in the north still worshipped God truly. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: "the hand of God" here means God's influence for good, not judgment. The king's order was based on a prophet's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Matthew Henry: God gave them the one heart. It is God who works "to will and to do." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- Poole: God inclined their hearts by the power of grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/30-12.htm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: "a very great assembly" is literally "a congregation in great multitude." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- The Expositor's Bible: the crowd was bigger than the festival crowds the Chronicler himself had seen. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/2-chronicles-30.html

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: these were the altars Ahaz set up "in every corner" (28:24), so the city was cleansed as well as the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Matthew Henry: they cleared away the idolatrous altars before keeping the feast. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: the priests and Levites were ashamed of having been slow to purify themselves (29:34). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- JFB: it was mainly the priests, shamed into action by the people's zeal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Barnes: the laggard priests had been held back either by lack of zeal or by leanings toward idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-chronicles-30.html
- Matthew Henry: they blushed to be outdone by ordinary people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/30-17.html

**v. 16**
- Barnes: normally the priest took the blood from the person offering. This time the Levites handed it on, because the worshippers were unclean. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-chronicles-30.html
- JFB calls this a departure from the established rules. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: the lambs would have been unclean if killed by unclean hands. At Josiah's Passover (2 Chronicles 35) the Levites did this as the normal rule, so Hezekiah's exception seems to have become the practice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Gill: the uncleanness came from idolatry or ceremonial causes, and there wasn't time to purify. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/30-17.html

**vv. 18–20: interpretations differ most here**
- **Traditional reading**
  - Enduring Word: they acted from ignorance, not rebellion. A prepared heart matters more than perfect ritual knowledge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-30/
  - Ellicott: "pardon" is properly "make atonement for" (*kipper*), as in Leviticus 16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/30.htm
  - Precept Austin cites a NET note on the root meaning of *kapar*. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary
- **How serious was the fault?**
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls it a real breach of God's order, less wicked than Uzziah's but able to provoke similar anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-30.html
  - JFB: it went against the law (Numbers 9:6) and was allowed only because Hezekiah prayed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/30.htm
  - Gill, labelled "Baptist · Calvinism" on StudyLight: they were sincere and came from far away, so the king chose to admit them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/30-18.html
  - Poole: they were so keen that they took the risk. A commentator on the same page (not named in the excerpt) thinks they were allowed in so they wouldn't be discouraged. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/30-18.htm
- **Heart versus ceremony**
  - The Geneva Study Bible: Hezekiah knew God values faith and sincerity more than ceremonies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_chronicles/30-18.htm
  - Matthew Henry adds a limit. Hezekiah didn't ask God to excuse a lack of sincerity. Seeking God is the "one thing needful." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/30-18.html
  - Constable: God pardoned ritual uncleanness when the heart was right. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-30.html
- **What "healed" means**
  - Matthew Henry: forgiveness, plus God accepting their worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/30-18.html
  - The Pulpit homiletics offers two options: bodily sickness that had begun or was feared, or sin seen as a moral sickness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_chronicles/30.htm
  - The NET translates it "forgave the people." https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/30-20.htm
- **Catholic text**: the Douay-Rheims renders v. 19 as God "will not impute it to them" that they weren't sanctified. https://biblehub.com/catholic/2_chronicles/30-18.htm

**v. 21**
- The Restoration Commentary: "loud instruments" means the larger, stronger-sounding instruments, played each day of the feast. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/2-chronicles-30.html

**v. 22**
- Barnes: "they ate" means they kept the feast. The Levites served every day. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-chronicles-30.html
- The Pulpit homiletics: Hezekiah encouraged all the Levites alike, gifted or not, which is a lesson for pastors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_chronicles/30.htm
- Matthew Henry: the peace offerings were a sign of fellowship with God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary

**v. 23**
- Barnes: the extra week was voluntary and a sign of zeal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/2-chronicles-30.html
- Constable: the feast went so well that it was extended. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-30.html

**v. 24**
- JFB: more priests consecrated themselves, so there were enough hands for the extra services. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/2Ch/2Ch_030.cfm
- Selman (quoted by Enduring Word on ch. 35): Josiah's offerings were more than double Hezekiah's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/

**v. 25**
- Selman (same page): Josiah's Passover seems to have had even more people than Hezekiah's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-35/

**v. 26**
- Constable: Josiah's Passover followed the law more strictly, but Hezekiah's was the greatest since Solomon in turnout and spiritual renewal. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-30.html
- Precept Austin: you have to go further back to find a Passover like Josiah's, because his was closer to God's Word. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-35-commentary

**v. 27**
- Precept Austin: God fulfilled the priests' blessing, and the joy came from obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-30-commentary
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary calls this a model reformation, ending in the priestly blessing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-30.html

**Things I couldn't find**
- **Tradition differences:** the clearest contrast is between Henry's "God works to will and to do" (v. 12) and Precept Austin's point that God responds to our choices (v. 9). Neither page ties this to a church tradition.
- **Missing sources:** I found nothing from Methodist, Pentecostal, Lutheran or Anglican sources, or from Bible Odyssey.
- **Other views:** Catholic and Orthodox commentary (beyond the Douay text) and prosperity, Word of Faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter weren't found, so they're left out.
